html:
Jayavarman VII was king of the Khmer Empire from 1181 until about 1218, and is often called the most powerful of the Khmer kings. He was a devout Mahayana Buddhist and the greatest builder Angkor ever had.

He was a prince of the royal family who spent years away from the capital, campaigning in Champa. In 1177 a Cham fleet sailed up the Mekong and the Tonle Sap and sacked Angkor. Jayavarman led the fight back, drove the Cham out and was crowned in 1181. Later in his reign his armies conquered Champa and held it for some years.

His works:

  • The walled city of Angkor Thom, with the Bayon at its centre, its towers carved with huge calm faces.
  • Large temple-monasteries such as Ta Prohm, dedicated to his mother, and Preah Khan, to his father.
  • A network of roads with rest houses for travellers.
  • More than a hundred hospitals, according to his inscriptions, which say he felt his subjects' illnesses more than his own.

With Buddhism as its guide, his rule has been described as an early welfare state. It also stretched the empire's labour and resources: his reign was the high point of Angkorian building, and few great temples came after. Under his successors there was a Hindu reaction, and many Buddha images were defaced. Modern Cambodia treats him as a national hero.
